ruling_text:
Motion for Attorney Fees
Before the Court is Defendants Kimberly Kovacs and MyJane, Inc.'s Motion for attorney's
fees pursuant to Civil Code §1717 and request for costs after dismissal of this action.
Facts
Plaintiffs Raquel Rodriguez and Frank Rodriguez sued Defendants Kimberly Kovacs,
MyJane, and MJIC Inc. dba Manifesteven for:
1. Fraudulent concealment
2. Fraud
3. Breach of fiduciary duty
4. Breach of contract
5. Breach of contract
6. Conversion
7. Unjust enrichment
8. Constructive trust
Trial was set for March 3, 2025. (ROA 157.)
On March 3, 2025, Plaintiffs failed to appear for trial. The trial date was vacated and the
Court set an OSC re dismissal for 4/21/25. (ROA 205.)
On April 21, 2025, the Court vacated the default against Defendant Manifesteven and
dismissed the action without prejudice. (ROA 215.)
On 4/28/25, Defense Counsel served a Notice of the dismissal. (ROA 217.)
On August 11, 2025, Defendants Kimberly Kovacs and MyJane filed this Motion for
attorney's fees. (ROA 223.)
Merits re Attorney's Fees
This Motion appears timely filed on 8/11/25. (ROA 223.) A motion claiming fees generally
must be served and filed within the time for filing a notice of appeal from the judgment
under Cal Rules of Court, rule 8.104 and 8.108 in an unlimited civil case, i.e., generally,
within 60 days after notice of entry of the judgment is mailed, or under Cal Rules of Court,
rule 8.822 (Jones v Goodman (2020) 57 Cal.App.5th 521, 541–542.) Here, the motion was
filed within 60 days of the notice of the dismissal.
Defendants seek attorney’s fees under Civil Code §1717.

There are two contracts at issue according to the FAC; only one - signed by Plaintiffs and
MyJane - contains an attorney’s fees clause.

On September 25, 2018, Kovacs (the CEO of MyJane) presented Rodriguez’ with a Keep It
Simple Security Agreement (KISS Agreement), wherein Rodriguez would loan $100,000
(One Hundred Thousand Dollars), to MyJane at eight percent (8%) interest. (FAC, ¶¶13, 17,
Ex. A.)

The Agreement is between the Rodriguez’s and MyJane. (FAC, Ex. A.) It was only signed by
Kovacs in her capacity as CEO.

While the KISS Agreement reflected Rodriguez’ payment of $100,000 for an eight percent
(8%) interest rate of return per annum [Exhibit A, §1(a)], the KISS Agreement was also a
convertible note allowing Rodriguez the option to either (1) remain creditors of MyJane
with a two times promise of return of their investment, plus interest at a rate of eight
percent (8%) after 18 months; or (2) upon certain conditions, Rodriguez could convert to
become equity owners of MyJane and receive shares in exchange for their $100,000 loan.
(FAC, ¶18.)

This Agreement has an attorney’s fees clause:

5.4 Costs, Expenses and Attorneys’ Fees; Indemnity. The Company hereby agrees,
subject only to any limitation imposed by applicable law, to pay all expenses,
including reasonable attorneys’ fees and legal expenses, incurred by the holder of
this KISS in endeavoring to collect any amounts payable hereunder which are not
paid when due, whether by declaration or otherwise (“Costs”). The Company
agrees that any delay on the part of the holder in exercising any rights hereunder
will not operate as a waiver of such rights. The holder of this KISS shall not by any
act, delay, omission or otherwise be deemed to have waived any of its rights or
remedies, and no waiver of any kind shall be valid unless in writing and signed by
the party or parties waiving such rights or remedies. If any action at law or in
equity is necessary to enforce or interpret the terms of this KISS, the prevailing
party shall be entitled to reasonable attorneys’ fees, costs and necessary
disbursements in addition to any other relief to which such party may be
entitled. The Company shall indemnify and hold the Investor harmless from any
loss, cost, liability and legal or other expense, including attorneys’ fees of the
Investor’s counsel, which the Investor may directly or indirectly suffer or incur by
reason of the failure of the Company to perform any of its obligations under this
KISS or any agreement executed in connection herewith; provided, however, that
the indemnity agreement contained in this Section 5.4 shall not apply to liabilities
which the Investor may directly or indirectly suffer or incur by reason of the
Investor’s own gross negligence or willful misconduct.
(FAC, Ex. A, emphasis added.)

Thus, as an initial matter, there is no contract signed by Defendant Kovacs. Further, the
FAC does not ask for attorney’s fees against her but only against MyJane. (See e.g. FAC,
¶109.) It does not appear that Defendant Kimberly Kovacs was a party to any written
agreement with an attorney’s fees clause.
The Court is therefore inclined to deny fees to her on that basis.

As to Defendant MyJane, it has shown that Plaintiffs sued to enforce the KISS contract in
the fourth cause of action and said contract contains an attorney's fees clause.

However, it is not clear to this Court that Defendant has shown it is the prevailing party.

California Civil Code section 1717(a) provides that in any action on a contract where the
contract specifically provides for attorney's fees, "the party who is determined to be the
party prevailing on the contract, whether he or she is the party specified in the contract or
not, shall be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees in addition to other costs" (Civ. Code §
1717). The statute requires the court to "determine who is the party prevailing on the
contract for purposes of this section, whether or not the suit proceeds to final judgment"
(Civ. Code § 1717). Importantly, section 1717(b)(2) states: "Where an action has been
voluntarily dismissed or dismissed pursuant to a settlement of the case, there shall be no
prevailing party for purposes of this section" (Civ. Code § 1717)

Neither of these procedures occurred.

However, the critical issue is whether a dismissal for failure to prosecute constitutes a
"voluntary dismissal" under section 1717(b)(2). A dismissal for failure to prosecute
imposed by the court is not a voluntary dismissal initiated by the plaintiff. The legislative
history demonstrates that the 1981 amendment was intended to allow defendants to
recover fees in failure-to-prosecute situations, distinguishing such dismissals from those
voluntarily requested by plaintiffs (Hsu v. Abbara (1995) 9 Cal.4th 863; Nasser v. Superior
Court (1984) 156 Cal.App.3d 52.).

On a party's noticed motion for attorney's fees, the judge must determine which party is
the party prevailing on the contract. (Civ. Code § 1717(b)(1); Regency Midland Constr., Inc.
v Legendary Structures, Inc. (2019) 41 Cal.App.5th 994, 1000; Burkhalter Kessler Clement &
George LLP v Hamilton (2018) 19 CA5th 38, 43. In ruling on the motion, the judge has the
discretion to make one of the following determinations:

(1) that a particular party has prevailed on the contract or
(2) that neither party has prevailed.

(DisputeSuite.com, LLC v Scoreinc.com (2017) 2 C5th 968, 973.)

A prevailing party for purposes of a cost award is not necessarily the prevailing party for
purposes of awarding contractual attorney fees. (Zintel Holdings, LLC v. McLean, (2012) 209
Cal. App. 4th 431, 438 & fn.1.) Rather, the prevailing party for contractual attorney fees
award purposes is the party who recovered greater relief in an action "on the contract."
(Civ. Code § 1717(b)(1); see Hsu v. Abbara (1995) 9 Cal. 4th 863.)

Here, Defendants argue that they are the prevailing parties because there was an
unqualified victory- they defeated all of the claims.

The action, however, was dismissed without prejudice.

Defendants cite Scott Co. of California v. Blount, Inc. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 1103, 1109 to argue
that when a party obtains a simple, unqualified victory by completely prevailing on or
defeating all contract claims in the action and the contract contains a provision for
attorney fees, section 1717 entitles the successful party to recover reasonable attorney
fees incurred in prosecution or defense of those claims. But the litigants in Scott went to
trial and a judgment was rendered.

A victory on the merits of the contractual dispute is not necessarily required before a judge
may make a fee award. A procedural victory that finally disposes of the dispute, such as an
involuntary dismissal with prejudice and without any likelihood of the same litigation being
refiled in another forum, may merit a prevailing party award of fees under Civ. Code §
1717. (DisputeSuite.com, LLC v Scoreinc.com (2017) 2 C5th 968, 981).

Defendant offers no argument or analysis of this issue.

But even if the Court were to find that Defendant is the prevailing party on the contract,
that would limit recovery to the time spent on the breach of contract claim as to the KISS
contract.

The judge may award the defendant attorney's fees incurred in defending against tort
claims joined with the contract claims when the provision for attorney's fees in the
contract is broad enough to encompass tort claims and the judge determines that the
defendant is the prevailing party with respect to these claims. (Santisias v Goodin, supra,
17
C4th at 608, 622 (provision awarding attorney's fees to "[t]he prevailing party in any
dispute arising out of this agreement" covers both contract and noncontract claims).

Civil Code § 1717 makes an otherwise unilateral (or one-sided) right to attorney's fees
under a contract a reciprocal right to ensure mutuality of remedy. It allows recovery of
attorney's fees by whichever contracting party prevails, even when the contract only
provides for recovery by one of the parties. (Santisias v Goodin (1998) 17 C4th 599, 610–
611; Hsu v Abbara (1995) 9 C4th 863, 870–871; Korchemniy v Piterman (2021) 68 CA5th
1032, 1049; Harris v Rojas (2021) 66 CA5th 817, 823 (primary purpose of CC § 1717 is to
ensure mutuality of remedy for fee claims under unilateral attorney fee provisions; this
statute is immaterial when provision is mutual.)

But here, the attorney's fees clause appears to be unilateral in favor of Plaintiffs. Section
1717 does not apply to make tort claims mutual. Defendant does not address this issue.

Moreover, even if Defendant was the prevailing party and the attorney's fees clause was
not unilateral in favor of Plaintiffs, it is a narrow clause that does not cover tort claims.
Defendant does not address this issue.

The contract language says that the prevailing party is entitled to fees only to "enforce or
interpret" the contract. The tort claims are not included based on this language. As our
Supreme Court has indicated, where a lease authorizes an award of attorneys' fees in an
action to "enforce any ... provision ... of this [contract]", tort claims are not
covered. (Santisias v. Goodin, supra, 17 Cal.4th at p. 622, fn. 9.) Other decisions are in
accord. (See, e.g., McKenzie v Kaiser-Aetna (1976) 55 Cal.App.3d 84, 89 ("an action for
negligent misrepresentation is not an action to enforce the provisions of a
contract"); Demirjian v. Ideal Heating Corp. (1949) 91 Cal.App.2d 505, 909–910 (lease
authorizing award of attorneys' fees in an action "to enforce lessor's rights hereunder"
does not include tort claims); Xuereb v. Marcus & Millichap, Inc. (1992) 3 Cal.App.4th 1338,
1342-1343 (attorneys' fees not permitted on tort claims under contractual provision
authorizing fees in an action to interpret or enforce the contract.)

Defendant argues that it is entitled to all fees spent on the entire case because they cannot
be apportioned. (Motion, p. 4:23-5:7; see Williams Decl. ¶ 18.) But Defendant has not
shown that the claims are inextricably intertwined and that fees could not be apportioned.

For all of these reasons, attorney’s fees are denied.

Merits re Costs
As a general rule, the prevailing party in a lawsuit is entitled to recover allowable costs.
(Code Civ. Proc., § 1032, subd. (b) (“[e]xcept as otherwise expressly provided by statute, a
prevailing party is entitled as a matter of right to recover costs in any action or
proceeding”).)

The costs memorandum must be served and filed within the earlier of:

• 15 days after the clerk’s service of notice of entry of judgment or dismissal
(under CCP § 664.5; or
• 15 days after any party’s service of such notice; or
• 180 days after entry of judgment. [CRC 3.1700(a)(1)]

The established procedure for recovering the costs allowed under section 1032 is to file
a cost memorandum, supported by a verified statement of counsel. (Code Civ. Proc., §
1034, subd. (a) (“[p]rejudgment costs allowable under this chapter shall be claimed and
contested in accordance with rules adopted by the Judicial Council”; California Rules of
Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1) (rule 3.1700).)

In such cases, “If the items on a verified cost bill appear proper charges, they are prima
facie evidence that the costs, expenses and services therein listed were necessarily
incurred,” and “[t]he normal procedure to challenge individual items is by a motion to
tax costs.” (Rappenecker v. Sea-Land Service, Inc. (1979) 93 Cal.App.3d 256, 266.) If no
timely motion to tax costs is filed, the court has no involvement with the cost award.
Instead, rule 3.1700(b)(4) states “the clerk must immediately enter the costs on the
judgment."

Here, there is no verified memorandum of costs filed. Defendant has cited no case to show
it can obtain costs without this mandatory procedure and a timely filed memorandum of
costs.

Thus, the Motion is denied.

Defendants are ordered to serve notice.
